title: Search Index Freshness
summary: Keeping a search index in sync with the source of truth, and living with the lag when it isn't — dual writes, CDC, and reindex strategies.

slides.markdown:
A search index is almost always a **derived copy** of data that lives in a primary database — which means every write to the database has to somehow make its way into the search index too. Get that sync wrong and users see stale or missing results; get it slow and there's a window where the database and search index simply disagree.

This topic covers the plumbing that keeps them in sync (dual writes vs CDC), how much lag is normal, and when a full reindex is unavoidable versus an incremental update will do.

There are two fundamentally different cadences for getting data into a search index.

| | Batch reindexing | Near-real-time indexing |
|---|---|---|
| Cadence | Scheduled (hourly, nightly) | Seconds after the write happens |
| Simplicity | Simple — one big job, easy to reason about | More moving parts — a continuous pipeline |
| Freshness | Data can lag by the whole batch interval | Lag measured in seconds |
| Good fit | Content that changes slowly (product catalogs, docs) | Content users expect to see instantly (a new post, a price change) |
| Resource pattern | Spiky — one big load, then idle | Steady, ongoing background load |

**How to decide:** batch is fine — and cheaper to build — wherever a few hours of staleness doesn't hurt the product. Reach for near-real-time only where users would actually notice the lag, since it's meaningfully more infrastructure to run correctly.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a write path that updates the DB and the search index
slides.markdown:
![Write path fanning out to the database and, via CDC, the search index](assets/index-freshness-pipeline.svg)

Every write path needs two destinations to end up consistent: the database (the source of truth) and the search index (a derived, denormalized copy). How those two updates happen — synchronously in the same request, or asynchronously via a separate pipeline — is exactly the dual-writes-vs-CDC decision on the next slide.

Notice the search index update is drawn as asynchronous even in the "near-real-time" case — true synchronous updates to both stores in one transaction are rare, because they'd tie the database's write latency to the search engine's.

assets.alt: Write path fanning out to the database and, via CDC, the search index

slides.sectionTitle: Keeping the index in sync: dual writes vs CDC-driven indexing
slides.markdown:
**Dual writes** mean the application code writes to the database and then separately writes to the search index, in the same request. It's simple to implement but fragile: if the second write fails after the first succeeds (a crash, a timeout, a bug), the two stores silently diverge with no automatic recovery.

**CDC (change data capture)** instead reads the database's own write-ahead log or replication stream and derives index updates from it, entirely outside the application's write path. Because it reads from the database's actual committed changes, it can't miss a write the way a failed second dual-write can — if the database recorded the change, CDC will eventually see it, even if the indexing pipeline is temporarily down.

CDC costs more infrastructure to set up (Debezium, a database's native change stream, or similar), but it's the standard choice in production because it structurally can't drift the way dual writes can.

slides.sectionTitle: Indexing lag: why search results can trail the source of truth
slides.markdown:
Even a well-built near-real-time pipeline has **indexing lag** — the delay between a write committing to the database and that change becoming visible in search. It comes from real, unavoidable steps: the change has to propagate through the CDC stream, get transformed into an indexable document shape, and get written into the search engine's index (which itself may only refresh its searchable view periodically, as Elasticsearch does by default).

This lag is usually seconds, not milliseconds — and that's a legitimate, accepted trade-off in most products, not a bug to chase to zero. The goal is bounding and monitoring the lag, not eliminating it (eliminating it entirely would mean synchronous writes to both stores, which most systems deliberately avoid for latency reasons).

slides.sectionTitle: Full reindex vs incremental reindex, and when each is needed
slides.markdown:
An **incremental reindex** updates just the documents that changed — the normal, ongoing mode of keeping an index fresh, whether via dual writes or CDC. A **full reindex** rebuilds the entire index from scratch, document by document, from the source of truth.

Full reindexes are needed in a specific set of situations: the index's schema or analyzer changes (a new field, a different tokenizer — old documents were never indexed with the new rules), index corruption or an unrecoverable divergence from the database, or migrating to a new search cluster entirely. They're expensive and slow on a large collection, so production systems build them to run without taking search offline — typically by building the new index in parallel and only swapping traffic over once it's caught up.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: dual writes to DB and index falling out of sync silently
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We write to the database, then write to the search index right after — if both calls are in our code, they'll stay in sync."

**Why it's wrong:** the two writes aren't atomic. If the process crashes, the request times out, or the search engine is briefly unavailable between the two calls, the database write succeeds and the index write is silently lost — with no error visible to the user and nothing forcing a retry. Over time, these small failures accumulate into a meaningfully stale or incomplete index, and nobody notices until a customer reports a missing search result.

**Correct model:** treat dual writes as inherently lossy and either add a reconciliation mechanism (a periodic diff-and-repair job comparing database and index) or move to CDC-driven indexing, which derives updates from the database's own durable log instead of a second application-level write that can fail independently.

slides.sectionTitle: Zero-downtime reindex: building the new index in parallel and swapping an alias
slides.markdown:
A full reindex of 50 million documents at 5,000 docs/sec takes roughly 2.75 hours — far too long to take search offline for. The standard pattern uses an **alias**: the application never queries an index by its literal name, only by an alias (e.g. `products-search`) that points at whichever index is currently live.

To reindex: build a brand-new index (`products-search-v2`) from the source of truth while the old one (`products-search-v1`) keeps serving all live traffic untouched. Once the new index is fully built and verified (spot-checked document counts, a handful of sample queries), atomically repoint the alias from v1 to v2 — a single metadata operation, not a data migration, so it's effectively instant and has no window where search is down or serving a half-built index.

The old index (v1) stays around briefly as a rollback target before being deleted, and CDC or dual-write updates during the rebuild need to be replayed into v2 too, or documents written during the multi-hour build window go missing from the new index the moment it goes live.

slides.sectionTitle: Tuning the refresh interval: a direct lag-vs-throughput knob
slides.markdown:
Many search engines don't make a written document searchable the instant it's indexed — Elasticsearch, for example, batches incoming writes and only makes them visible to queries on a periodic **refresh**, 1 second by default. Setting `refresh_interval` to `30s` instead means writes queue up for up to 30 seconds before becoming searchable, but the engine does dramatically less work overall, since each refresh has real fixed overhead (rebuilding in-memory search structures) that's now amortized across far more documents per refresh.

A bulk-loading job indexing millions of documents typically disables refresh entirely (`refresh_interval: -1`) for the duration of the load, then re-enables it once done — turning what would be millions of tiny refresh operations into effectively one, at the cost of nothing being searchable at all until the load finishes and refresh resumes.

This is the same freshness-vs-throughput trade-off that shows up everywhere in this topic, expressed as a single tunable number: tighter refresh means fresher results and more overhead; looser refresh means cheaper indexing and more lag.
